summary: A medicine for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s dementia that blocks NMDA receptors in the brain. It is not a sedative and not a cure; it can help steady symptoms, but can cause confusion, dizziness and (rarely) hallucinations while the dose is being raised.
description: Memantine is used in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s dementia to help slow the worsening of symptoms and support day-to-day function. It is not a fast-acting calming medicine and it won’t reverse dementia, but it can steady the course for some people—especially when combined with a cholinesterase inhibitor (such as donepezil). The main things to watch for are dizziness, confusion, sleep problems, and flare-ups of agitation, delusions or hallucinations, particularly during dose increases or in Lewy body dementia.
patient_summary: Memantine is for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s dementia. It doesn’t work overnight and it doesn’t “fix” memory, but some people seem steadier over weeks—less decline, a little more function, sometimes fewer behavior flare-ups. The tradeoff: dizziness and confusion are common early on, and a small group can get more agitated or even hallucinate (especially while the dose is being raised or with Lewy body dementia). Don’t stop it suddenly unless there’s a serious reaction—step down slowly.

primary.context: FDA-indicated for moderate-to-severe dementia of the Alzheimer type. It’s often used when symptoms have progressed beyond “mild,” either alone or layered on top of a cholinesterase inhibitor for a combined approach.

off_label.context: Sometimes used in Lewy body dementia, but people with this condition can be very sensitive: hallucinations, delusions and agitation can get worse—especially while the dose is being raised.
Used off-label in Parkinson disease dementia. Monitor closely for worsening confusion, sleep disruption, or hallucinations.
Sometimes considered when blood-vessel disease is part of the dementia picture, usually as an add-on rather than on its own.
Evidence supports memantine as a glutamate-targeting option for hair-pulling in adults, with improvement over placebo in an 8-week randomized trial.
Also studied for skin-picking (excoriation) disorder in adults, with meaningful symptom improvement in an 8-week randomized trial.

therapeutic_response.display: Hours: The medicine is absorbed and reaches peak levels (immediate-release peaks at about 3–7 hours; extended-release at about 9–12 hours); Days: Side effects (dizziness, confusion) often show up early—especially while the dose is being raised; Weeks: Benefit is usually judged over several weeks (dementia care) or over about 8 weeks in trials for body-focused repetitive behaviors; 60–80 hours: It stays in the body a long time (half-life), so changes, including side effects, can linger after a dose change

common_adverse_effects.notes: This is a big one—especially early. The risk of falls matters in dementia. If dizziness is strong, the dose can be raised more slowly, or held longer before the next increase.
Often shows up early and may fade with time. If headaches are persistent or severe, reassess dosing and hydration, and rule out other causes.
It may seem odd, but some people get more confused while the dose is being raised. Dose increases can trigger it. If confusion gets much worse, pause the increases or step back to the last dose.
Memantine isn’t designed as a sedative, but sleepiness can happen. If daytime sleepiness increases, consider morning dosing (and make sure nothing else sedating was added).
More likely in people with Lewy body dementia or baseline hallucinations. If hallucinations worsen after an increase, treat it like a medication signal—not a behavior problem.
Some people feel more on edge while the dose is being raised. If anxiety or agitation builds up, slow down or check with the prescriber whether memantine is helping overall.

serious_risks.risk: Severe worsening of mental state: agitation, delusions, hallucinations, sudden confusion (delirium)—especially in some types of dementia or while the dose is being raised
Seizures (reported): higher caution in people with seizure history

Fainting, slow heartbeat, heart failure and heart-rhythm changes (prolonged QT) have been reported after approval: get checked if you faint, feel your heart racing or pounding, or have new heart symptoms
Severe hypersensitivity reactions (rare): including Stevens-Johnson syndrome—urgent evaluation for rash or mucosal symptoms
Acute kidney injury (postmarketing reports): assess if sudden decline, dehydration, or medication interactions are present
Suicidal ideation (reported): monitor mood and safety, especially if neuropsychiatric symptoms shift

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to memantine or any component of the formulation

precautions: Neuropsychiatric effects can occur: confusion, dizziness, drowsiness, sleep disturbance; less commonly agitation, delusions, hallucinations
Higher risk of neuropsychiatric worsening in Lewy body dementia or in people with baseline hallucinations
Kidney problems raise the amount of medicine in the body—the dose may need to be changed
Alkaline urine reduces clearance (levels rise) and can increase side effects
Use caution in seizure disorders (seizures have been reported)
Use caution with heart disease (high or low blood pressure, slow heartbeat and fainting have been reported)

interactions.interactant: NMDA antagonist stacking (amantadine, ketamine; caution also with high-dose dextromethorphan)
interactions.mechanism: Additive NMDA-related effects can increase confusion, dizziness, and psychotomimetic symptoms (agitation, hallucinations).
interactions.action: Avoid combining them without a clear need. If overlap can’t be avoided, raise the dose more slowly and watch closely for changes in behavior, mood or thinking.

interactions.interactant: Urine alkalinizing agents or conditions (eg, sodium bicarbonate, major dietary shifts toward alkalinization)
interactions.mechanism: Alkaline urine significantly reduces memantine clearance, increasing blood levels and side effects (confusion, dizziness, agitation).
interactions.action: Use caution. If alkalinization is needed medically, consider dose adjustment and tighter monitoring.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS-active medications (sedatives, anticholinergics, polypharmacy in dementia)
interactions.mechanism: Not a classic “dangerous combo,” but additive cognitive burden can look like memantine intolerance (confusion, falls, sleep disruption).
interactions.action: If side effects show up, review the whole med list—memantine is often blamed when polypharmacy is the real driver.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Cognitive function over time (trend matters more than a single score)
Functional outcomes: Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) and Instrumental ADLs (IADLs)
Changes in behavior and mental state: agitation, irritability, sleep problems, delusions, hallucinations—especially while the dose is being raised or in Lewy body dementia
Falls and steadiness when walking (dizziness or unsteadiness is a safety risk)
Renal function for dosing decisions (use Cockcroft-Gault for adjustment in many clinical settings)
Blood pressure and heart symptoms if you have heart disease (high or low blood pressure, risk of fainting)
Ophthalmic monitoring when clinically indicated (Canada recommends periodic ophthalmic exam; consider if corneal symptoms or eye disease are present)

special_populations.pregnancy: There is little information in people; harm was seen in some animal studies. It should be used in pregnancy only if the possible benefit outweighs the possible risk.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known whether memantine is present in human breast milk. The manufacturer advises weighing infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and the mother’s treatment benefit. If used, monitor the infant for unusual sleepiness, feeding problems, or irritability.
special_populations.geriatric: Adult doses apply, but watch more closely for dizziness, falls, confusion, sleep problems and changes in behavior or mental state—especially while the dose is being raised.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose changes are often needed with kidney problems; the amount in the body rises a lot as kidney function falls. The extended-release form is generally avoided with dialysis or similar kidney treatment (CRRT).
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Mild-to-moderate impairment: no adjustment. Severe impairment: limited data; use with caution (Canada: not recommended).

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Partially hepatic; primarily independent of CYP enzymes; forms 3 metabolites with minimal activity
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (~74%); ~48% unchanged; active tubular secretion with pH-dependent reabsorption

dosing.titration: Memantine is titrated slowly to reduce side effects—especially confusion and dizziness. For dementia, it’s a weekly step-up schedule to a target dose. For hair-pulling/skin-picking, dosing is typically 10 mg/day then 20 mg/day after 2 weeks (adult data).

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Stopping memantine abruptly can backfire—some people worsen cognitively or behaviorally, and a subset can develop withdrawal-like symptoms (confusion, hallucinations, delusions, insomnia, increased anxiety and agitation). Unless there’s a severe adverse reaction, step it down gradually.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Memantine is best known for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s dementia. In psychiatry land, the “why” is usually neuropsychiatric: cognition and function, plus the behavioral volatility that comes with dementia. Separately, memantine has real evidence as an off-label option for body-focused repetitive behaviors like hair-pulling and skin-picking.
items: {link:condition:alzheimer-disease:Moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s dementia}: Helps slow symptom progression and support function over time
Behavioral volatility in dementia: Not a sedative, but sometimes part of a plan when agitation/irritability are riding shotgun with cognitive decline
{link:condition:trichotillomania:Trichotillomania (hair-pulling)}: Off-label option with randomized trial evidence
{link:condition:excoriation-disorder:Skin-picking (excoriation) disorder}: Off-label option with randomized trial evidence
off_label: Dementia with Lewy bodies / Parkinson disease dementia (variable results; higher neuropsychiatric sensitivity)

Not a miracle—more like the chaos dial got turned down a notch.

quotes: The first few weeks were messy—more confusion before it settled.
It felt like my thinking got worse for a bit, then leveled out.
We had a rough patch during the dose increases.
items.note: Transient confusion is more likely during dose increases and in severe dementia.

quotes: Sleep got weird—more tossing and turning.
I got jumpier and more agitated when we increased the dose.
We saw more hallucinations and had to back off.
items.note: Agitation, delusions, and hallucinations can occur—especially in Lewy body dementia or in people with baseline hallucinations.

quotes: The urge didn’t disappear, but it stopped bossing me around.
I had more ‘pause’ between the urge and the behavior.

items.note: In trials for body-focused repetitive behaviors, dosing was typically 10–20 mg/day over 8 weeks.

sections.intro: This med has two storylines: dementia care and compulsive behaviors. Either way, it’s not a “feel it in an hour” medication. People usually notice changes over weeks—and sometimes the first thing they notice is side effects.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Memantine isn’t a PRN medication and it’s not built for instant calm. Blood levels rise within hours, but the real-world changes (function, behavior, compulsive symptoms) are typically tracked over weeks.
key_points: Hours: The medication is absorbed and reaches peak levels (IR peaks ~3–7 hours; XR peaks ~9–12 hours)
Days: Side effects (dizziness, confusion) often show up early—especially during titration
Weeks: Clinical benefit is usually assessed over several weeks (dementia care) or over ~8 weeks in body-focused repetitive behavior trials
60–80 hours: Long half-life means changes (including side effects) can linger after dose changes

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: For hair-pulling and skin-picking, memantine has surprisingly strong signal in an 8-week randomized, double-blind trial: about 6 in 10 people on memantine were rated “much” or “very much” improved, compared with under 1 in 10 on placebo. That’s the kind of difference patients actually feel.
sections.metric: Much/Very Much Improved at 8 Weeks (Trichotillomania / Skin-Picking Disorder)
sections.clinical_details: In a double-blind 8-week study of 100 adults with trichotillomania or skin-picking disorder, participants received memantine (10–20 mg/day) or placebo. Memantine produced significantly greater improvement on the NIMH symptom severity scale and functional impairment measures. At endpoint, 60.5% of the memantine group were “much” or “very much” improved versus 8.3% on placebo (NNT ≈ 1.9).

citation.authors: Grant JE, Chesivoir E, Valle S, Ehsan D, Chamberlain SR
citation.title: Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Study of Memantine in Trichotillomania and Skin-Picking Disorder

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: If confusion, agitation, or hallucinations spike—especially during dose increases—take it seriously. Sometimes the fix is simply slowing down or stepping back the dose.
other: Neuropsychiatric effects can occur: confusion, dizziness, drowsiness, sleep disturbance; less commonly agitation, delusions, hallucinations
Higher risk of neuropsychiatric worsening in Lewy body dementia or in people with baseline hallucinations
Renal impairment increases exposure—dose adjustments may be needed
Alkaline urine reduces clearance (levels rise) and can increase side effects
Use caution in seizure disorders (seizures have been reported)
Use caution in cardiovascular disease (hypertension/hypotension, bradycardia, syncope have been reported)
patient_counseling: Titrate slowly. Most problems happen during dose increases, not at a stable dose.
Report new or worsening hallucinations, delusions, agitation, or sudden confusion—especially if the person has Lewy body dementia.
If dizziness or falls increase, pause and reassess the dose. Safety > speed.
Tell your clinician if kidney function is reduced—dosing often needs adjustment.
Avoid major alkalinizing changes without medical guidance (certain meds, supplements, and dietary shifts can raise urine pH and raise memantine levels).
Don’t stop abruptly unless there’s a severe reaction—step down gradually to avoid rebound symptoms.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: dizziness, headache, and confusion. It can also push sleep in the wrong direction and, in a smaller group, worsen agitation or hallucinations—particularly during titration or in neuropsychiatrically sensitive dementias.
plain_language_list: Confusion or increased disorientation (common, often titration-related)
Drowsiness or fatigue (can happen, but this is not primarily a sedative)
Agitation, delusions, hallucinations (less common but clinically important)

More likely in people with Lewy body dementia or baseline hallucinations. If hallucinations worsen after an increase, treat it like a medication signal—not a behavior problem.
Some people feel more keyed up during titration. If anxiety or agitation ramps up, slow down or reassess whether memantine is a net win.

sections.intro: Memantine doesn’t run through CYP the way many psych meds do, but it has two interaction “lanes” that matter: (1) stacking NMDA-like agents and (2) anything that alkalinizes urine and slows memantine clearance.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping memantine abruptly can backfire—some people worsen cognitively or behaviorally, and a subset can develop withdrawal-like symptoms (confusion, hallucinations, delusions, insomnia, increased anxiety and agitation). Unless there’s a severe adverse reaction, step it down gradually.
key_points: Avoid abrupt discontinuation except for severe adverse reactions (eg, serious rash, severe neuropsychiatric decompensation clearly tied to the medication).
If stopping, use a gradual taper: either cut the dose ~50% and hold for about 4 weeks between reductions, or step down using available dose strengths.
An alternative taper is weekly decrements down to the lowest dose: decrease by 5 mg/day (immediate release) or 7 mg/day (extended release) at weekly intervals until the lowest dose, then discontinue.
If the condition clearly worsens after withdrawal, consider re-initiation—especially if the decline tracks closely with discontinuation.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Memantine is titrated slowly to reduce side effects—especially confusion and dizziness. For dementia, it’s a weekly step-up schedule to a target dose. For hair-pulling/skin-picking, dosing is typically 10 mg/day then 20 mg/day after 2 weeks (adult data).

adult.alzheimer_ir_titration: Increase total daily dose by 5 mg each week as tolerated to 20 mg/day; may give once daily or in 2 divided doses when >5 mg/day
adult.alzheimer_ir_max: 20 mg/day (10 mg PO BID or 20 mg once daily per clinician preference/tolerability)
adult.alzheimer_xr_titration: Increase by 7 mg weekly as tolerated to 28 mg once daily
adult.trichotillomania_skin_picking_titration: Increase to 20 mg PO once daily after 2 weeks if tolerated
adult.renal_impairment_ir: CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment. CrCl 30 to <50: start 5 mg once daily; titrate by 5 mg no more often than weekly; some people may need a reduced max due to higher exposure. CrCl <30: start 5 mg once daily; after ≥1 week if tolerated, target 5 mg BID.
adult.renal_impairment_xr: CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment. CrCl 30 to <50: start 7 mg once daily; titrate by 7 mg no more often than weekly; some people may need a reduced max due to higher exposure. CrCl <30: start 7 mg once daily; after ≥1 week if tolerated, target 14 mg once daily.
adult.dialysis: Not likely significantly dialyzable. Hemodialysis/peritoneal dialysis/CRRT: immediate-release dose as if CrCl <30 mL/min; extended-release: avoid use.
adult.hepatic_impairment: Mild-to-moderate: no adjustment. Severe: limited data; use with caution (Canada: not recommended).
adult.geriatrics: Use adult dosing, but go slower if confusion, falls, or neuropsychiatric symptoms flare during titration.
adult.conversion_ir_to_xr: Start ER the day after the last IR dose. If current IR is 10 mg/day, convert to ER 14 mg once daily. If current IR is 20 mg/day, convert to ER 28 mg once daily.
adult.missed_doses: If several days are missed, restart at a lower dose and retitrate rather than jumping back to the previous dose.
adult.administration: May take with or without food. ER capsules may be swallowed whole or opened and sprinkled on applesauce and swallowed immediately (do not chew/crush/divide). Oral solution should be measured with the provided device and slowly squirted into the corner of the mouth; do not mix with other liquids.

sections.simple_explanation: This is a slow-and-steady titration medication. The goal is to reach a therapeutic dose without triggering a confusion/agitation spiral. If side effects show up, the fix is usually not “push through”—it’s “slow down.”

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Memantine isn’t a go-to medication in pregnancy or breastfeeding because human data are limited. In older adults with dementia (the most common use case), dosing is the same as adults—but tolerability rules everything. Kidney function changes the dose.
sections.pregnancy: Human data are limited; adverse events have been observed in animal reproduction studies. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
sections.lactation: It is not known whether memantine is present in human breast milk. The manufacturer advises weighing infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and the mother’s treatment benefit. If used, monitor the infant for unusual sleepiness, feeding problems, or irritability.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing, but monitor more aggressively for dizziness, falls, confusion, sleep disturbance, and neuropsychiatric changes—especially during titration.
sections.hepatic: Mild-to-moderate impairment: no adjustment. Severe impairment: limited data; use with caution (Canada: not recommended).
sections.renal: Dose adjustments are commonly needed in renal impairment; exposure rises substantially as kidney function declines. Extended-release is generally avoided in dialysis and CRRT-type settings.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Cognitive function over time (trend matters more than a single score)
Functional outcomes: Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) and Instrumental ADLs (IADLs)
Neuropsychiatric symptoms: agitation, irritability, sleep disturbance, delusions, hallucinations—especially during titration or in Lewy body dementia
Falls and gait stability (dizziness/ataxia = safety risk)
Renal function for dosing decisions (use Cockcroft-Gault for adjustment in many clinical settings)
Blood pressure and cardiovascular symptoms in people with cardiac disease (hypertension/hypotension, syncope risk)
Ophthalmic monitoring when clinically indicated (Canada recommends periodic ophthalmic exam; consider if corneal symptoms or eye disease are present)

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Memantine comes in immediate-release tablets and solution, plus extended-release capsules. The formulation choice is usually about convenience (once daily vs divided dosing) and tolerability (some do better with slower release).
items: Oral Solution (memantine HCl): 2 mg/mL; also labeled as 10 mg/5 mL presentations exist depending on product
Extended-Release Capsules (memantine HCl ER): 7 mg, 14 mg, 21 mg, 28 mg
Titration packs may exist historically; availability varies by market and manufacturer

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Memantine blocks NMDA-type glutamate receptors in a way that matters most when the system is overactivated. The concept is excitotoxicity: too much glutamate signaling can keep NMDA channels “open” too long, driving excess calcium influx and neuronal stress. Memantine sits in the channel (at the magnesium site) with a longer dwell time than magnesium, acting like a gate that closes down excessive stimulation while preserving more normal signaling. Mechanistically, it also binds with low affinity to the PCP site at the NMDA receptor—one reason a small subset of patients can experience agitation, delusions, or hallucinations, especially if the brain is already prone to dopamine/glutamate imbalance.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Memantine is a standard option once Alzheimer’s dementia is moderate to severe. It’s often used alone or paired with a cholinesterase inhibitor when the goal is function and stability, not “symptom elimination.” From a psychiatry perspective, the key is behavior: dementia symptoms often come with agitation, sleep disruption, paranoia, or hallucinations, and memantine can be either a stabilizer or a trigger depending on the person. Separately, for trichotillomania and skin-picking disorder, memantine is an evidence-based off-label option that targets glutamate rather than serotonin—often considered when first-line behavioral approaches and/or SSRIs haven’t been enough.

faqs.q: What is memantine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: Most commonly: moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s dementia (which is absolutely part of psychiatry because cognition and behavior live together). Off-label, memantine also has solid evidence for trichotillomania (hair-pulling) and skin-picking (excoriation) disorder.

faqs.q: Will memantine calm agitation or help sleep?
faqs.a: Sometimes it helps indirectly if the overall dementia picture stabilizes, but memantine is not a sedative and it’s not a PRN “calm down” medication. In some people—especially during titration—it can actually worsen agitation or disrupt sleep. If agitation spikes right after a dose increase, slow down.

faqs.q: How long does memantine take to work?
faqs.a: Blood levels change within hours, but symptom changes are usually judged over weeks. For hair-pulling/skin-picking, the key study tracked outcomes over 8 weeks. For dementia care, clinicians usually look at trends over several weeks to months.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Dizziness, headache, and confusion are the big three. Constipation or diarrhea can happen too. Neuropsychiatric effects like agitation or hallucinations are less common, but they’re the ones you don’t ignore.

faqs.q: Can memantine cause hallucinations or make confusion worse?
faqs.a: Yes. Hallucinations and worsening confusion are reported, and risk can be higher in Lewy body dementia or in people who already hallucinate. It also tends to show up during titration—so if symptoms worsen after a dose increase, consider holding or stepping back rather than pushing forward.

faqs.q: What dose is used for trichotillomania or skin-picking?
faqs.a: A common approach is 10 mg once daily, then increase to 20 mg once daily after 2 weeks if tolerated. That matches the typical dosing used in clinical research for these conditions.

faqs.q: Do you have to adjust the dose for kidney disease?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The amount of memantine in the body rises as kidney function falls. With more severe kidney problems, target doses are lower (for example, immediate-release may target 5 mg twice daily; extended-release may target 14 mg once daily). The extended-release form is generally avoided with dialysis or CRRT.

Try not to—unless there’s a severe reaction. Stopping suddenly can lead to worse thinking and memory or a rebound of symptoms (confusion, hallucinations, trouble sleeping, anxiety or agitation). Stepping down gradually is usually safer.

It doesn’t have the major liver-enzyme interactions that many psychiatric medicines have, but the real-world issue is that several medicines together can add up and affect thinking. If confusion or falls increase, review the full medicine list—not just memantine.

faqs.q: What should I watch for while the dose is being raised?
faqs.a: A sudden jump in confusion, agitation, sleep disruption, dizziness, or hallucinations—especially right after a dose increase. If that happens, slow down, hold the dose longer, or step back. The goal is stability, not speed.

faqs.q: Is memantine a cure for Alzheimer’s?
faqs.a: No. It doesn’t reverse dementia. The realistic goal is slowing decline and supporting function and behavior for some people—often as part of a bigger plan that includes safety, routines, caregiver support, and (sometimes) other medications.
